concepts.title: Caching Strategies and Invalidation
concepts.description: A cache buys speed by keeping a second, faster copy of data. The hard part is knowing when that copy has gone stale and what to do about it.
learningObjectives: Explain why caching improves latency and reduces load on the system of record, and identify what makes data a good or bad caching candidate.
Implement and explain the cache-aside (lazy-loading) pattern, including its behavior on a cache miss.
Implement and explain the write-through pattern and contrast it with write-around and write-back.
Explain the core invalidation problem and compare TTL-based expiry with explicit invalidation.
Diagnose a stale-cache bug and identify which caching pattern or invalidation strategy would have prevented it.

sections.heading: Why Cache: Trading Staleness for Speed
sections.body:
A cache keeps a second, faster-to-read copy of data closer to where it's needed, typically in memory (Redis, Memcached, or an in-process cache), while the disk-backed database remains the system of record. You gain speed and take load off the database. You pay with a copy that can go out of sync.

That trade is worth making when access is read-heavy, when the underlying data is expensive to compute or query but cheap to serve once cached, and when a *little* staleness is tolerable. It's a bad idea when data must always be current (an account balance checked right before authorizing a withdrawal) or when the workload is write-heavy with few repeated reads, since entries would be invalidated before anyone reads them. The hit rate tells you which side you're on: at a 95% hit rate the database sees one read in twenty, and at 20% you have added a network hop to every request to save very little. Decide which category a piece of data falls into before reaching for a cache.

sections.heading: Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading)
sections.body:
In the **cache-aside** pattern, the application checks the cache first on every read. On a hit, it returns the cached value without touching the database. On a miss, it falls back to the database, reads the real value, populates the cache with it, and then returns it. The cache is passive: it doesn't know how to load data, so the application owns all of the loading logic, and the cache sits beside the main data path, not in front of it.

The advantage is that the cache only holds data somebody has requested, which works well when access is skewed toward a "hot" subset, the common case. It has a well-known failure mode: if a very popular key expires and a burst of concurrent requests all miss on it, they can all fall through to the database at once. This is the "thundering herd" or "cache stampede" problem; an example below shows it along with the standard mitigation.

sections.heading: Write-Through, Write-Around, and Write-Back
sections.body:
**Write-through** caching updates the cache and the database together, synchronously, on every write. A read right after the write sees the new value. The cost is extra write latency (two writes have to succeed instead of one) and a cache filled with keys that might never be read again. The two writes aren't one transaction, so decide what happens when the database write succeeds and the cache write fails; deleting the key, with a TTL behind it, is the usual answer.

**Write-around** sends writes straight to the database, bypassing the cache, which only gets filled the cache-aside way on a later read. This avoids spending cache space and write time on keys that might never be read again. If the key was already cached, though, the old value stays there until its TTL runs out, so write-around is normally paired with deleting the key on write; the next read then takes a miss.

**Write-back** (or write-behind) writes to the cache first, acknowledges success to the caller immediately, and asynchronously flushes to the database later. This is the fastest write path of the three, but data is lost if the cache node crashes before the flush completes. Use it for data that can tolerate that, like counters or analytics buffers, and keep it away from durable transactional records.

sections.heading: The Core Problem: Invalidation
sections.body:
There's an old joke that there are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation, naming things, and off-by-one errors. **TTL (time-to-live) expiry** is the simplest invalidation strategy: every cached entry automatically expires after a fixed duration, bounding how stale it can get without the writer needing to know who is caching what. The cost is that data can remain stale for up to the full TTL after a change.

**Explicit invalidation** means deleting or updating the cache entry as part of the write path. It tightens the staleness bound considerably, but every writer has to remember to invalidate every cache key its data affects. Miss one path and, without a TTL, that entry stays stale with no upper bound. There is also a race even when nobody forgets: a reader misses and loads the old row, a writer updates the row and deletes the key, and then the slow reader stores the old row. Because of both problems, many systems combine the two: explicit invalidation on the known write paths, plus a TTL that bounds the worst case.

sections.heading: Choosing Combinations, and What Breaks
sections.body:
As a starting default, cache-aside plus a TTL is the simplest combination, appropriate for read-heavy workloads that can tolerate brief staleness. Cache-aside plus explicit invalidation suits data where staleness must be minimized and the write paths are few and well-known. Write-through earns its cost when read-after-write consistency matters and the extra write latency is acceptable. Write-back is reserved for high-volume, loss-tolerant scenarios where write speed dominates every other concern.

One failure mode cuts across all of these combinations: a code path that writes to the database *without* going through the invalidation or write-through logic the rest of the system relies on, such as a batch job, an admin tool, or a second service that touches the same table. This "second writer" problem is a frequent cause of "impossible" stale-cache bugs. When one appears, first ask "is there another writer we forgot about?" If there are too many writers to police, invalidate from the database's change log (change data capture, with a tool such as Debezium), which sees every committed write whoever made it.

examples.title: Cache-Aside in Practice
examples.code:
# Fragment: `cache` and `database` stand for your own client wrappers
CACHE_TTL_SECONDS = 300  # 5 minutes

def get_user_profile(user_id):
    cache_key = f"user_profile:{user_id}"
    cached = cache.get(cache_key)
    if cached is not None:
        return cached  # cache hit -- fast path, database never touched

    # cache miss -- fall back to the system of record
    profile = database.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = %s", user_id)
    cache.set(cache_key, profile, ex=CACHE_TTL_SECONDS)
    return profile
examples.explanation: The application owns the "if miss, load and populate" logic, and the cache is unaware that a database exists. Nothing tells the cache "the underlying row changed" unless the application clears `cache_key` in the write path, so the TTL (`ex=CACHE_TTL_SECONDS`) is what bounds the staleness here. Two details matter in production. If the user doesn't exist, the query returns `None`, which looks the same as a miss, so every request for that id goes to the database; a scraper walking through made-up ids can bypass your cache completely. Cache a "not found" marker for a short time to prevent it. And if every entry gets the same TTL after a deploy warms the cache, they all expire together, so add a random amount (jitter) to each one.

examples.title: Write-Through vs. Write-Around
examples.code:
# Fragment: pseudocode for the SQL; continues the previous example
# WRITE-THROUGH: every write updates the database AND the cache together
def update_user_profile_write_through(user_id, new_data):
    database.execute("UPDATE users SET ... WHERE id = %s", user_id, new_data)
    cache.set(f"user_profile:{user_id}", new_data, ex=CACHE_TTL_SECONDS)
    # with no concurrent writer, the very next read sees new_data

# WRITE-AROUND: writes bypass the cache entirely
def update_user_profile_write_around(user_id, new_data):
    database.execute("UPDATE users SET ... WHERE id = %s", user_id, new_data)
    cache.delete(f"user_profile:{user_id}")
    # next read is a guaranteed MISS -- cache-aside logic repopulates it,
    # but only once someone actually asks for it again
examples.explanation: Without concurrent activity, both leave the cache and database in agreement once the write completes. They differ in what happens to keys that are rarely read after being written. Write-through always pays the cost of writing them into the cache, which is wasted work and memory for cold keys (a bulk import of profiles nobody looks at for months, for example). Write-around, paired with cache-aside for reads, only caches keys somebody asked to read, at the cost of one miss on the next read after a write. Write-around uses `cache.delete` so that only one place, the miss-fill code, knows how to build a cache entry; in the write-through version, `new_data` must already have the same shape as the row the read path stores, or readers see two formats. Delete is also safer under concurrency. With write-through, two writers can commit to the database in one order and reach the cache in the other, leaving the wrong value there until the TTL. Delete is idempotent, so its order doesn't matter, though a slow reader can still put back an old value it loaded before the write. The TTL covers that remaining case.

examples.title: The Thundering Herd / Cache Stampede
examples.code:
Setup: cache_key "trending_products" has TTL=60s, is read by ~2,000 req/s
        (a very hot key -- shared by nearly every request)
        The query behind it takes about 1 second.

t=60.000s: TTL expires, key is evicted
t=60 to 61s: 2,000 requests arrive, ALL miss the cache
           (the first query hasn't finished, so nothing has repopulated it)
        -> all 2,000 requests fall through to the database
        -> database, which normally serves this query rarely (once/60s),
           is running ~2,000 identical queries at once -- can fall over

FIX (single-flight / lock-based repopulation):
  on miss for "trending_products":
    if NOT acquire_lock("trending_products:refresh", ttl=5s):
        return stale_copy_if_kept()  # or wait briefly and retry the read
    value = database.query(...)
    cache.set("trending_products", value, ex=60)
    release_lock("trending_products:refresh")
examples.explanation: A hot key's expiry turns one query per minute into about 2,000 at once. The pile-up size is request rate times query time, so the same key with a 50 ms query would stack up about 100, and the slow queries you most wanted to cache are the ones that stampede worst. The fix funnels concurrent misses on the key through a lock so one request queries the database and repopulates the cache, while the others wait briefly or serve the previous value. Serving the previous value means keeping it: store the entry with a long real TTL and a shorter "refresh after" time inside it, because once Redis expires a key the old value is gone. Two more details: the lock needs its own TTL, so a crashed refresher doesn't block everyone, and it should only be released by the holder that acquired it. Refreshing hot keys in the background before they expire avoids the problem, and TTL jitter keeps many keys from expiring together.

misconceptions.description: Adding a cache is basically free performance, with no downside besides needing more infrastructure.
misconceptions.clarification: Caching introduces a second copy of the truth, and with it bugs that don't exist without the cache: stale reads, thundering herds on expiry, and "second writer" paths that bypass invalidation. It also adds a new dependency (the cache itself) that needs to be available, sized correctly, and monitored; a cache outage that isn't handled gracefully (no fallback to the database, or a fallback that isn't rate-limited) can turn a performance optimization into a full outage. If the database can no longer carry the load without the cache, the cache has become part of your availability.

misconceptions.description: As long as I set a TTL, I don't need to think about explicit invalidation, because the cache will fix itself.
misconceptions.clarification: A TTL only bounds how long staleness can last, it doesn't prevent it, and for some data (a price change that must show immediately, or a permissions change that must take effect right away for security reasons) "stale for up to N seconds" is not acceptable. TTL-only is fine when the business can live with bounded staleness. When it can't, you need explicit invalidation on the write path, with the TTL kept as a safety net for paths that get missed, or you skip the cache for that read.

exercises.prompt: A product page uses cache-aside with a 120-second TTL for its price field, and has no explicit invalidation on write. A pricing admin updates a product's price at 10:00:00. Predict what price different users see when reading the page at 10:00:30, 10:01:00, and 10:02:30, assuming the page had been read (and cached) at 09:59:00, just before the update.
exercises.code:
09:59:00 - page read, price=$40 cached, TTL=120s (expires 10:01:00)
10:00:00 - admin updates price in database to $50 (no cache invalidation call made)
10:00:30 - user reads page
10:01:00 - cache entry from 09:59:00 expires
10:02:30 - user reads page
hints: Cache-aside only repopulates the cache on a MISS. Has the cache entry from 09:59:00 missed yet by 10:00:30?
Work out when the cached entry expires, given it was set at 09:59:00 with a 120s TTL.
After the TTL boundary passes, what does the NEXT read actually do -- and what price does the database have at that point?
exercises.expectedAnswer: 10:00:30 -> $40 (stale). The cache entry set at 09:59:00 doesn't expire until 10:01:00, so it's still a hit at 10:00:30, returning the old cached price even though the database was already updated to $50 at 10:00:00. 10:01:00 -> $50 (the entry expires at 10:01:00, so a read at that instant or later is a miss that loads $50 from the database). 10:02:30 -> $50 (fresh). The 09:59:00 entry is long gone, so this read either misses and loads $50 itself, or hits an entry that an earlier reader repopulated with $50.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Because there's no explicit invalidation on the write path, the cache has no way to learn that the price changed at 10:00:00. It serves what it cached at 09:59:00 until that entry's TTL runs out, whatever happens to the underlying row. The entry expires at 10:01:00 (09:59:00 plus 120 seconds), so the 10:00:30 read is a hit on stale data, and every customer between 10:00:00 and 10:01:00 could see the wrong price: 60 seconds here. Had the page been cached one second before the update, the stale window would have been 119 seconds, nearly the full TTL. The 10:02:30 read comes after expiry, so either it misses and loads $50 itself, or it hits an entry another reader loaded after 10:01:00, which is also $50. If a window of up to two minutes costs money (complaints, incorrect checkouts), add explicit invalidation to the admin update path, and have checkout read the price from the database.

exercises.prompt: A team implements write-through caching for user permission flags, believing it guarantees the cache is always fresh. A support ticket reports that after an admin revokes a user's access via a separate internal admin tool (not the main application), the user retains access in the main app for several minutes. Find the gap and fix it.
exercises.code:
# Fragment: `cache` and `database` stand for your own client wrappers
# MAIN APPLICATION -- write-through, looks correct in isolation
def update_permissions(user_id, new_permissions):
    database.execute("UPDATE permissions SET ... WHERE user_id = %s", user_id, new_permissions)
    cache.set(f"permissions:{user_id}", new_permissions, ex=600)

def check_access(user_id, action):
    permissions = cache.get(f"permissions:{user_id}")
    if permissions is None:
        permissions = database.query(  # returns a list of permission names
            "SELECT permission FROM permissions WHERE user_id = %s AND revoked = false",
            user_id
        )
        cache.set(f"permissions:{user_id}", permissions, ex=600)
    return action in permissions

# SEPARATE INTERNAL ADMIN TOOL (different codebase, same database)
def revoke_access_from_admin_tool(user_id, permission):
    database.execute(
        "UPDATE permissions SET revoked = true WHERE user_id = %s AND permission = %s",
        user_id, permission
    )
    # (does not touch the cache at all)
hints: Write-through only makes the cache coherent for writes that actually GO THROUGH that write-through code path. Does the admin tool call update_permissions?
The admin tool writes directly to the same database table. From the main app's cache's point of view, did anything happen at all?
This is the "second writer" problem -- think about what needs to happen on EVERY code path that can modify this data, not just the one you wrote write-through for.
exercises.solutionCode:
# FIX 1 (preferred): make every writer invalidate the shared cache key
def revoke_access_from_admin_tool(user_id, permission):
    database.execute(
        "UPDATE permissions SET revoked = true WHERE user_id = %s AND permission = %s",
        user_id, permission
    )
    cache.delete(f"permissions:{user_id}")  # force the main app to reload on next check

# FIX 2 (safety net, use alongside Fix 1, not instead of it):
# lower the TTL for security-sensitive data so the worst-case staleness window
# is small even if an invalidation path is missed again in the future.
PERMISSIONS_TTL = 30  # was 600

def update_permissions(user_id, new_permissions):
    database.execute("UPDATE permissions SET ... WHERE user_id = %s", user_id, new_permissions)
    cache.set(f"permissions:{user_id}", new_permissions, ex=PERMISSIONS_TTL)

def check_access(user_id, action):
    permissions = cache.get(f"permissions:{user_id}")
    if permissions is None:
        permissions = database.query(  # returns a list of permission names
            "SELECT permission FROM permissions WHERE user_id = %s AND revoked = false",
            user_id
        )
        cache.set(f"permissions:{user_id}", permissions, ex=PERMISSIONS_TTL)
    return action in permissions
exercises.solutionExplanation: Write-through only keeps the cache coherent for writes that pass through the code path that updates both the database and the cache. The admin tool updates the same `permissions` table through different code and has no idea the main application has a cache, let alone what its keys are called. As far as the cache knows, nothing happened at revoke time, so it keeps serving the old permissions for up to the full 600-second TTL. This is the "second writer" problem: a different service, an admin tool, a batch job, or a console session can modify data without going through the caching logic, and write-through cannot protect against writers it doesn't know about. The fix is to make the admin tool invalidate the key and, because this data is security-sensitive, also shorten the TTL so the next forgotten writer costs 30 seconds and not ten minutes. Both `cache.set` calls need the shorter TTL: changing only the one in `update_permissions` would leave entries loaded by `check_access` at 600 seconds. A better long-term design puts all permission changes behind one service that both applications call.

assessments.prompt: A hot cache key expires and 3,000 concurrent requests all miss at the same instant, sending 3,000 simultaneous identical queries to the database, which then falls over. What is this failure pattern called, and what is a standard mitigation?
options: Thundering herd (cache stampede); mitigated by having only one request refresh the cache (e.g. via a lock or single-flight) while others wait or serve a stale value.
Cache coherence violation; mitigated by increasing the cache's memory allocation.
Split-brain; mitigated by adding a quorum requirement to cache reads.
Write amplification; mitigated by switching from write-through to write-around.
assessments.explanation: The expiry of a heavily shared key makes every concurrent reader miss at once and fall through to the database, multiplying one query into thousands. The standard fix funnels concurrent misses on the same key through a lock or single-flight mechanism so one request repopulates the cache while the rest wait briefly or serve a slightly stale value. The “Write amplification; mitigated by switching from write-through to write-around” option names an unrelated concept (write amplification is about storage engines and SSDs writing more bytes than the application asked for). The “Cache coherence violation; mitigated by increasing…” option is about copies that disagree; here no copy exists, and more memory doesn't stop simultaneous misses. The “Split-brain; mitigated by adding a quorum requirement…” option describes two nodes both acting as leader during a network partition, which has nothing to do with expiry.

assessments.prompt: Explain the difference between cache-aside and write-through caching, including a concrete scenario where you'd prefer one over the other.
assessments.modelAnswer: Cache-aside (lazy loading) puts the application in charge of the cache on the read path: check the cache first, and only on a miss does the application fetch from the database and populate the cache with what it just fetched. The cache is passive: it knows nothing about writes unless the application tells it to invalidate or update a key. Write-through updates the cache on the write path: every write goes to the database and the cache together, synchronously, so a read after the write completes sees the new value (as long as all writers use that path and concurrent writers don't reach the cache out of order). The tradeoff is about which keys end up cached and how fresh they are after a write. Cache-aside only caches data that has been requested, which is efficient when access is skewed toward a hot subset, such as a content site where most traffic hits a few popular pages. Without invalidation it leaves a staleness window after a write, bounded by the TTL. Write-through suits reads that must be correct right after a write, such as a user who updates their profile and expects the change on the next page load. It pays by populating the cache for every write, including data that might never be read again, and it makes every write slightly slower and dependent on the cache. In practice, I'd reach for cache-aside as the default for read-heavy, write-light data where brief staleness after a rare write is tolerable (product descriptions), and write-through when writes are relatively infrequent but must be immediately visible on the next read from any instance (a user's own settings, where seeing your own change matters more than the write-time cost).

assessments.prompt: Which workload is the worst candidate for adding a cache?
options: A read-heavy workload where the same expensive query is repeated by many users.
A read-heavy workload where the underlying data is expensive to compute but rarely changes, where many different readers request the same small set of results all day.
A write-heavy workload with very few repeated reads, where cached entries would be constantly invalidated and rewritten with almost nothing ever being read from them.
A workload where a small number of popular keys account for most of the traffic.
assessments.explanation: A write-heavy workload with few repeated reads keeps invalidating and rewriting entries nobody reads, so the cache adds work on every write and almost never saves a query. The “A read-heavy workload where the same expensive…”, “A read-heavy workload where the underlying data…”, and “A workload where a small number…” options all describe good candidates: read-heavy, expensive to compute but cheap to serve, or skewed toward a hot subset of keys, which is where cache-aside does well.

assessments.prompt: Why is write-back (write-behind) caching generally reserved for data like counters or analytics buffers, rather than durable transactional records?
options: Write-back is slower than write-through for every operation, so it's only used where write latency doesn't matter.

Write-back acknowledges the write to the caller before the data is flushed to the database, so if the cache node crashes before that flush completes, the write can be lost entirely, a risk tolerable for counters or analytics but not for durable records.
Write-back requires a database that supports write-through, which counters typically lack.
Write-back is identical to write-around, and the two terms are used interchangeably.
assessments.explanation: Write-back writes to the cache, acknowledges success, and flushes to the database later. If the cache node crashes before the flush, the caller believes a write happened that the database never received. Losing a few increments of a view counter is tolerable; losing an order is not. The “Write-back requires a database that supports write-through…” option invents a requirement: the flush is an ordinary database write. The “Write-back is slower than write-through for every…” option is backwards: write-back is the fastest write path of the three. The “Write-back is identical to write-around…” option is false; write-around and write-back are distinct patterns with opposite behavior on the write path (write-around bypasses the cache; write-back writes to it first).

assessments.prompt: A caching strategy that looks correct on paper (explicit invalidation on the application's main write path, plus a TTL as backup) still produces stale-cache bugs in production. What is the first, most likely explanation to investigate?
options: TTL-based expiry and explicit invalidation can never be combined, so one of them must be misconfigured.
The cache's hardware is failing intermittently.
The database itself has a bug causing it to return incorrect data.
There is a "second writer".
assessments.explanation: A "second writer" is a batch job, admin tool, or other service that changes the same rows without going through the invalidation code. The main write path can be flawless and the cache still goes stale until the TTL. The “The cache's hardware is failing intermittently” option would show up as errors and misses, not as old values. The “TTL-based expiry and explicit invalidation can never…” option is false: combining both is common, because the TTL bounds the damage when an invalidation is missed. The “The database itself has a bug causing…” option is far less likely than an application path that skips invalidation, and a quick query against the database rules it out.

assessments.prompt: After adding a Redis cache in front of the product database, users sometimes see stale prices for minutes after an update, and when the cache restarted, the database fell over. How would you redesign the caching?
assessments.modelAnswer: Stale prices come from cache entries that outlive the data: with cache-aside and only a long TTL, updates do not reach the cache. Invalidate or update the key when the price changes (delete on write, or write-through), keep TTLs short for volatile data, and for prices consider whether checkout should always read the source of truth. The outage after restart is a thundering herd or cache stampede: every request missed at once and hit the database. Protect against it with request coalescing so only one request rebuilds a key, staggered TTLs with jitter, warming hot keys before taking traffic, and keeping Redis highly available (replicas, persistence). Add rate limiting or a circuit breaker in front of the database, and monitor hit rate and database load so the cache is treated as a critical dependency.

concepts.title: Database Scaling: Replication vs. Sharding
concepts.description: When a single database can no longer keep up, you can copy the data (replication) or split it (sharding). They solve different bottlenecks at different costs, and large systems often use both.
learningObjectives: Explain what replication solves (read capacity, availability) and what it structurally cannot solve (write capacity, total data size).
Explain what sharding solves (write capacity, total data size beyond one machine) and the new problems it introduces (cross-shard queries, rebalancing, choice of shard key).
Compare leader-follower replication with multi-leader and leaderless replication at a conceptual level, and state the main tradeoff each makes.
Evaluate a candidate shard key for a given workload and identify hotspot or cross-shard-query risks.
Explain replication lag concretely and connect it to the consistency tradeoffs covered in the CAP theorem concept.

sections.heading: Read-Bound or Write-Bound?
sections.body:
A database can hit two different bottlenecks, and they call for different fixes. The first is too much *read* traffic for one machine to serve, which replication targets. The second is too much *write* traffic, or too much total *data*, for one machine, which sharding targets.

So the first diagnostic question is: am I read-bound, or write/size-bound? Adding read replicas doesn't raise write throughput, because every write still goes through the leader and every replica has to apply it too. More copies of a firehose don't make the firehose flow faster. And sharding a database whose only problem is heavy reads gives you cross-shard queries, rebalancing, and no simple single-node transactions, when a few replicas or a cache would have done. Check the metrics before choosing: CPU split between SELECTs and writes, disk write latency, WAL or binlog volume, and the size of the hot data compared with RAM.

sections.heading: Replication: Leader-Follower, Multi-Leader, Leaderless
sections.body:
**Leader-follower** (primary-replica) replication is the common default: one node accepts all writes and propagates them to follower nodes, which serve reads and can be promoted to leader if the original one fails. It's the simplest to reason about, because there's a single, well-defined order in which writes happen.

**Multi-leader** replication allows more than one node to accept writes, commonly one leader per data center, improving write availability and latency across regions. It introduces write conflicts: if two leaders accept different, concurrent writes to the same record, something has to reconcile them once the writes propagate. Last-write-wins is the easy rule, and it discards one user's change without telling anyone; merging per field or asking the user keeps both.

**Leaderless** (Dynamo-style, quorum-based) replication lets any node accept reads or writes; a client or coordinator writes to, and reads from, a quorum of nodes. This trades away a single ordering of writes for higher availability and tunable consistency. How many nodes must answer each read and write becomes a number you configure, and that number is your CAP choice.

sections.heading: Replication Lag
sections.body:
**Replication lag** is the delay between a write being applied on the leader and becoming visible on a follower. It comes from network transfer, the time the follower takes to apply the write, and backlog when write volume is high or a long query blocks replay. It isn't a bug; any replication that isn't synchronous has it.

Lag produces two very common bugs. The **read-your-own-writes** problem: a user updates their profile, the page reloads, the reload request gets load-balanced to a lagging replica, and the user sees their own change vanish. The **monotonic-read violation**: a user reads a value, refreshes, and sees an *older* value than before, because the second read happened to hit a more-lagged replica than the first one did. Standard mitigations route a user's own reads to the leader (or a replica known to be caught up) for a short window after they write, pin a session to one replica so its reads don't go backward, or accept the lag where nobody would notice.

sections.heading: Sharding: Splitting Data Across Machines
sections.body:
**Sharding** (or partitioning) splits a large dataset and its write traffic across independent database nodes called shards, each holding a disjoint subset of the data, determined by a **shard key** (for example, `user_id`, hashed and assigned to a shard). This raises total write capacity and total storage beyond what one machine can hold, because shards do not all hold the same data: each handles its own slice, so write load is divided, where replication copies it.

A good shard key does two things: it needs to distribute load evenly (sharding by something like `signup_date` piles all of "today's" write traffic onto one shard, creating a hotspot), and it should, ideally, align with your most common query patterns. Queries that only need one shard's data are cheap; queries that need to gather data from every shard ("cross-shard" or "fan-out" queries) are expensive, as slow as the slowest shard, and give up most of the convenience a single database offers, including easy global secondary indexes, cross-shard joins, and cross-shard transactions.

sections.heading: Combining Both, and What Gets Harder
sections.body:
Large-scale systems typically combine both levers: shard the data across N nodes to handle write and size scale, then replicate each individual shard for read scale and availability within that shard. This adds operational complexity. **Resharding**, splitting or moving shards as data grows unevenly, is hard and risky, usually requiring dual-write or backfill migrations to avoid data loss or downtime mid-move. A common precaution is to create many more logical shards than machines at the start (say 1,024 logical shards on 4 nodes), so that growing means moving whole logical shards and no key is ever rehashed. Cross-shard transactions and joins either get pushed into the application layer or are avoided through the data model: denormalization, or a shard key that keeps related data together on one shard.

That cost is why sharding usually comes last, after query tuning, vertical scaling, replication, and caching. Some databases (Citus, Vitess, CockroachDB, Cassandra, DynamoDB) do the routing and rebalancing for you, but you still choose the key, and a bad key hurts there too.

examples.title: Diagnosing the Bottleneck: Read-Bound vs. Write-Bound
examples.code:
System A metrics:
  Reads: 50,000/sec      Writes: 200/sec      Data size: 80 GB
  CPU-bound on the single database, almost entirely from SELECT queries

System B metrics:
  Reads: 800/sec         Writes: 45,000/sec     Data size: 6 TB, growing 200GB/week
  CPU and disk I/O-bound, mostly from UPDATE traffic and sheer data volume
examples.explanation: System A is read-bound and its data fits comfortably on one machine, the profile replication is built for: add read replicas, route the 50,000 reads/sec across them, keep a single leader handling the light 200 writes/sec. Sharding would add cross-shard complexity for little gain, because write volume is low and 80 GB is small. System B is the opposite: write volume and data size are the constraints, and no number of read replicas increases how fast one leader can accept writes or how much one machine can store, because every replica applies the same writes and stores the full dataset. Sharding splits both. The numbers tell you more if you multiply them out. 45,000 writes/sec is about 27 billion a week, and 200 GB of growth spread over those is about 7 bytes each, so most of System B's writes must be updates to existing rows. Before sharding, check whether those updates can be batched or coalesced. At 200 GB a week the data also grows about 10 TB a year, so a shard count chosen for today's 6 TB will be too small within a year.

examples.title: A Shard Key Gone Wrong: The Hotspot Problem
examples.code:
BAD SHARD KEY: signup_date (e.g. shard = hash of the day a user signed up)
  -> every new signup today lands on the SAME shard as every other signup today
  -> that shard absorbs 100% of today's write traffic -- a hotspot
  -> yesterday's shard, and all older ones, sit nearly idle by comparison

BETTER SHARD KEY: hash(user_id) mod num_shards
  -> each user_id hashes to a pseudo-random shard, roughly uniformly
  -> new signups are spread evenly across ALL shards, not concentrated on one
  -> most queries (e.g. "get user 4821's orders") only need to hit ONE shard,
     because the key used to shard (user_id) is also the key most queries filter by
examples.explanation: Sharding by signup_date feels intuitive because it's a natural, ordered key, but it sends all signup writes to whichever shard owns "today" while the others idle. Hashing a well-distributed key like user_id spreads them, and it also matches the most common queries in a typical application, which are scoped to "this user", so most reads and writes touch one shard. Even distribution alone isn't enough: "show all orders placed in the last hour across all users" against a user_id-sharded database has to fan out to every shard and merge the results. No key is best for every query, so choose for the dominant ones. The `mod num_shards` form has a weakness of its own: going from 8 to 9 shards moves about 8/9 of all rows. Production systems map keys to a large fixed number of logical shards, or use consistent hashing, so that adding a node moves only its share. And if one user is enormous (a celebrity, a big tenant), even a hashed key gives that user's shard a hotspot.

examples.title: Replication Lag Causing a Read-Your-Own-Write Bug
examples.explanation: The bug rarely shows up in manual testing, because lag on a lightly loaded replica is often a few milliseconds, less than the redirect takes. It appears in production once write volume grows. The fix leaves the lag in place and works around it for the case users notice, reading what they just wrote. For a few seconds after a write, that user's reads go to the leader; everyone else's stay on the replica pool. The 10 seconds is a bet that lag stays below it. If a replica falls a minute behind, the bug returns, so monitor lag and take badly lagging replicas out of the read pool. A stricter version records the leader's log position at write time (an LSN in Postgres, a GTID in MySQL) and reads only from a replica that has replayed past it.

misconceptions.description: If reads are slow, sharding the database will help, since it splits the data into smaller pieces.
misconceptions.clarification: Sharding splits data by key across independent nodes, but a query that is slow because of a missing index or poor design is usually slow on each shard too, and a query that doesn't filter on the shard key now has to run on all of them. Sharding does divide single-shard reads, but its reason to exist is write throughput or data size beyond one machine, and it brings costs (cross-shard queries, rebalancing, no single-node transactions across shards) that read scaling doesn't require. Check indexes and query plans first. If the problem is too many reads for one machine, read replicas are the far cheaper fix.

misconceptions.description: Read replicas mean I always have a fully up-to-date, consistent backup copy of my data at all times.
misconceptions.clarification: Asynchronous replicas lag behind the leader, often by milliseconds but potentially much more under load, network issues, or resource contention, so a replica's data is a view slightly in the past. People conflate two uses. For read scaling, a small lag is often an acceptable price for much more read capacity and availability. As a backup, a replica that's lagging (or that faithfully replicates a destructive mistake, like an accidental DELETE, moments after it happens on the leader) is not a substitute for point-in-time backups or snapshots.
misconceptions.fact: Asynchronous replicas lag behind the leader, often by milliseconds but potentially much more under load, network issues, or resource contention, so a replica's data is a view slightly in the past.

exercises.prompt: A system adds 10 read replicas to its single-leader database, going from 1 database node to 11 total (1 leader + 10 replicas). Write throughput was the bottleneck, sitting at 100% capacity on the leader before this change. Predict what happens to write throughput and to read latency after this change, and explain why.
exercises.code:
BEFORE: 1 node (leader), write capacity saturated at 100%, read latency high due to
        read queries competing with writes for the same node's resources
AFTER:  1 leader + 10 read replicas, ALL writes still go through the single leader,
        reads are now distributed across the 10 replicas
hints: Every one of the 10 replicas still needs to receive and apply every single write that happens on the leader. Does adding replicas change how many writes the LEADER itself has to originally accept and process?
Separate the two workloads: what changed for reads, and what changed for writes -- are they affected the same way by this change?
If writes were already the bottleneck, is there anything about spreading OUT reads that touches the leader's write capacity at all?
exercises.expectedAnswer: Write throughput does not improve in any lasting way: every write still has to be accepted and processed by the same single leader, however many replicas exist downstream. Read latency likely improves significantly, since reads that used to compete with writes for the leader's resources are now served by the 10 replicas. That frees some leader CPU and I/O, which may help writes modestly, but it doesn't raise the leader's write ceiling. The change fixes read latency and leaves the reported bottleneck, write capacity, roughly where it was.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Replication only distributes reads. Every replica is a full copy that must apply every write, so replica count doesn't change the volume of writes, and the leader is still the only node accepting them. Replicas even add a little work, since the leader streams its log to each one (ten streams here; cascading replication moves some of that off the leader). The team may see a secondary improvement from less read contention on the leader. How much depends on how much of that 100% was reads, which is worth measuring before buying ten replicas. For more write capacity, reduce the write volume (batch, defer non-critical writes, drop unused indexes), move to a bigger leader, or shard so that several nodes accept writes.

exercises.prompt: A team shards their orders table by order_id, hashed evenly across 8 shards, expecting balanced load. In production, all 8 shards run at similarly high CPU, and growing from 4 shards to 8 barely lowered the load per shard. Their most common query, by far, is 'get all orders for a given customer_id.' Diagnose why adding shards didn't help and why this query is unexpectedly expensive, and propose a fix.
exercises.code:
Shard assignment: shard = hash(order_id) % 8
Most common query: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?
  -- since orders for one customer have essentially random order_ids,
  -- this query has no way to know which shard(s) hold this customer's orders
hints: Hashing order_id evenly across shards is good for distributing rows, but check whether it matches the field your most common query filters by.
If a customer's orders are scattered across all 8 shards essentially at random, what does the database have to do to answer 'get all orders for customer X'?

High CPU on every shard and the expensive query might be two symptoms of the same design choice. If every query runs on every shard, how many queries per second does each shard see with 4 shards? With 8?
exercises.solutionCode:
Better shard key: shard = hash(customer_id) % 8
  -- now every order belonging to the same customer lands on the SAME shard
  -- "get all orders for customer_id X" becomes a single-shard query again,
  --  hitting one shard instead of fanning out to all 8

(If order_id is still needed for lookups by order_id alone, maintain a small
 secondary index/lookup table mapping order_id -> customer_id or shard number,
 rather than re-sharding by order_id.)
exercises.solutionExplanation: Both symptoms have the same cause. Because orders are sharded by order_id, a customer's orders are scattered across all 8 shards, so every "get all orders for customer X" query has to run on all 8 shards and merge the results. Each shard therefore receives the full query rate: at 2,000 of these queries per second, every shard handles 2,000 per second with 4 shards, with 8, or with 80. Adding shards shrinks the index each one searches but not the number of queries it parses, plans, and answers, so CPU barely moves. Latency suffers too, since each request waits for the slowest of 8 shards. Re-keying on customer_id, the field the dominant query filters by, puts a customer's whole history on one shard. The same 2,000 queries per second now average 250 per shard, and doubling the shards halves that. The cost is a new risk: a business account with a huge order history makes its shard hotter than the rest, so check the largest customers before migrating. Distributing rows evenly was never the goal; distributing work is, and that depends on the queries.

assessments.prompt: A database is write-bound: a single leader node is at 100% CPU capacity from INSERT/UPDATE traffic, while read traffic is light. Which change increases write capacity?
options: Enable a CDN in front of the application servers.
Shard the data across multiple independently-writable nodes, so write traffic is divided among them rather than all funneling through one leader.
Increase the TTL on the application's caching layer.
Add more read replicas to the existing leader.
assessments.explanation: Sharding is the only listed change that divides write load across nodes that each accept writes independently: each shard handles its own slice of the data, so total write capacity grows with the number of shards. The “Add more read replicas to the existing leader” option is a common but ineffective response: every replica still applies every write the leader accepts, so replicas leave the leader's write ceiling where it was and help reads, which were light. The “Increase the TTL on the application's caching layer” option reduces database reads and leaves every write where it is. The “Enable a CDN in front of the application servers” option helps reduce load on application/web servers for content that can be cached at the edge, and has no effect on database write throughput.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a teammate why 'we're scaling the database' can mean two very different things (replication and sharding) and how to tell which one a situation calls for.
assessments.modelAnswer: Replication and sharding solve different bottlenecks, even though both get called "scaling the database." Replication makes multiple full copies of the same data, with one node (the leader, in the common leader-follower setup) accepting writes and propagating them to the others, which mainly serve reads. It's good for two things: increasing how much read traffic the system can serve, since reads can be spread across many copies, and increasing availability, since a follower can be promoted if the leader fails. What it cannot do is increase write capacity or total storable data size, because every replica has to apply the same stream of writes and hold the same full dataset. Sharding splits the data itself into disjoint pieces spread across independent nodes, typically by hashing or ranging some shard key. Because each shard only holds and processes its own slice of the data, both write throughput and total storage capacity increase as you add shards. Of the two tools, only sharding raises those ceilings. The cost is complexity: choosing a shard key that both distributes load evenly and matches your dominant query patterns, handling queries that need data from multiple shards (which lose the simplicity of a single-node query or transaction), and the operational difficulty of resharding as data grows unevenly over time. So ask: is the system struggling to serve enough reads (replication's job), or to accept enough writes or store enough data on one machine (sharding's job)? Sharding a read-bound system, or adding replicas to a write-bound one, adds cost and leaves the bottleneck in place. And if the metrics point at a few bad queries, fix those before doing either.

assessments.prompt: In multi-leader replication, two data-center leaders each accept a different, concurrent write to the same record before either write has propagated to the other. What does this scenario require that leader-follower replication does not?
options: A shard key, since this is fundamentally a sharding problem rather than a replication one.
Nothing extra -- multi-leader replication automatically serializes concurrent writes across leaders in the order they were issued.
A conflict-resolution mechanism to reconcile the two divergent writes once they propagate to each other.
A rollback of one of the two data centers to a previous backup, since concurrent writes across leaders cannot be reconciled any other way.
assessments.explanation: When two leaders accept different, concurrent writes to the same record, something has to reconcile them once they propagate. With leader-follower, one leader orders all writes, so this conflict can't occur. The “Nothing extra -- multi-leader replication automatically serializes…” option is false: neither leader knew about the other's write when it accepted its own, so there was no moment to put them in order. The “A shard key, since this is fundamentally…” option confuses this with sharding, which splits data where replication copies it. The “A rollback of one of the two…” option overstates the fix: one record needs reconciling, and restoring a data center would discard every unrelated write since the backup.

assessments.prompt: Following the "BAD SHARD KEY: signup_date" example, why does hashing by signup_date create a hotspot even though every user is assigned to some shard?
options: Because every user who signs up on the same day lands on the same shard.
Because hashing by date is computationally slower than hashing by user_id, causing that shard's CPU to run hot.
Because sharding by any date field is impossible; only numeric IDs can be used as shard keys.
Because signup_date is not a valid data type to hash, so the hashing function fails and defaults all traffic to shard 0.
assessments.explanation: Each day does map to some shard, so over a year the rows look well spread. But all of today's signups have the same date, so today's writes all go to one shard while the others sit nearly idle. Load is uneven in time even when the rows are even in total. The “Because hashing by date is computationally slower…” option is wrong: hashing either value takes well under a microsecond, nowhere near enough to matter next to a database write. The “Because signup_date is not a valid data…” and “Because sharding by any date field…” options are both fabricated: dates can be hashed like any other value, and shard keys don't have to be numeric.

assessments.prompt: A team treats their read replicas as their disaster-recovery backup strategy, reasoning "we always have multiple up-to-date copies of the data." Why is this risky?
options: Replicas only replicate schema changes, not the underlying data, so they are never useful for recovery.
Replicas are read-only, so no backup strategy can ever use them for any purpose.
Replication lag guarantees replicas are always more up to date than the leader, which makes them unsuitable as backups.

A replica lags behind the leader by some amount and will faithfully replicate destructive mistakes (like an accidental DELETE) shortly after they happen on the leader, so it is not a substitute for point-in-time backups or snapshots.
assessments.explanation: A replica copies everything, including an accidental DELETE, within moments, so every "backup" loses the rows together. It can also be missing the last few writes when the leader dies. Only point-in-time backups or snapshots let you go back to before the mistake. The “Replicas are read-only, so no backup strategy…” option is false: backups are often taken from a read-only replica to spare the leader. The trouble is treating the replica itself as the backup. The “Replicas only replicate schema changes…” option misstates replication, which copies the data as well as the schema. The “Replication lag guarantees replicas are always more…” option is backwards: replicas lag behind the leader and are never ahead of it.

concepts.title: Consistency Tradeoffs at Scale: Eventual vs. Strong
concepts.description: Every distributed data store, once it has more than one copy of anything, has to pick a consistency model. 'Is this consistent?' can only be answered with more questions: consistent in what sense, how quickly, and at what cost?
learningObjectives: Define strong consistency and eventual consistency, and place them as points on a spectrum rather than a binary.
Explain the mechanisms (quorum reads/writes, synchronous vs. asynchronous replication) that let a system move along that spectrum.
Connect consistency choices back to the CAP theorem's availability tradeoff during a partition, and to replication lag from the database-scaling concept.
Evaluate a real feature (a like count, a bank transfer, a comment thread) and recommend an appropriate consistency level with justification.
Explain read-your-own-writes and monotonic-read consistency as practical middle-ground guarantees weaker than strong consistency but stronger than plain eventual consistency.

sections.heading: Consistency Is a Spectrum
sections.body:
"Is the system consistent?" is an underspecified question. The useful version is: how strong a guarantee does this operation need, and what does the system provide? From weakest to strongest: **Eventual consistency**: given enough time with no new writes, all replicas converge to the same value, with no promise about how long that takes or what you might see in the meantime. **Read-your-own-writes** (session consistency): a user is guaranteed to see their own writes, even if other users might briefly see stale data. **Monotonic reads**: a user's successive reads never go backward in time, even if they're not fully current. (These two sit in the middle; neither implies the other, and a store can offer one, both, or neither.) **Strong consistency** (linearizability): every read reflects the most recent write, system-wide, as if there were only one copy of the data.

The top of the list is not always what you want. Each step toward stronger consistency costs something, and the next sections cover how you buy it and what you pay.

sections.heading: Moving Along the Spectrum: Quorums and Sync vs. Async Replication
sections.body:
One lever is the quorum: with N replicas, a write can require acknowledgment from W of them before returning success, and a read can require querying R of them and taking the most recent value seen. If W + R > N, the sets of replicas touched by any write and any read are guaranteed to overlap by at least one node, so a read that follows a completed write sees it. This is the quorum from the CAP lesson, and it gets a leaderless store close to strong consistency. It falls short of full linearizability in some cases: concurrent writes, a write that failed partway but still reached one replica, or conflicts resolved by clocks that disagree.

In leader-based systems the lever is the replication mode: **synchronous replication** (the leader waits for a follower to confirm before acknowledging the write to the client) means that follower is never missing an acknowledged write, at the cost of write latency and, per CAP, availability during a partition, since the leader can't get that confirmation if it can't reach the follower. Check what "confirm" means in your database: by default a synchronous Postgres standby confirms that the write is on its disk, so a query there can still miss it for a moment, unless you set `synchronous_commit = remote_apply`. **Asynchronous replication** (the leader acknowledges immediately, replicates in the background) gives low write latency and keeps working through partitions or slow followers, at the cost of the replication lag and staleness from the previous lesson. Reads from asynchronous followers are eventually consistent; reads from the leader are not affected.

sections.heading: Matching the Guarantee to the Feature
sections.body:
Stronger consistency generally costs latency or availability, so work out how much each feature needs. A bank balance or transfer needs strong consistency: approving a withdrawal against a stale balance loses money, which is worth the extra latency to prevent. A "like" count or view count can be eventually consistent, because nobody notices if it's off by a few for a couple of seconds, and the read/write volume is often too high to justify coordination. A user's own comment needs at least read-your-own-writes, since posting a comment and not seeing it feels broken, while other users seeing it a second later is fine.

Match the guarantee to the operation instead of maximizing it. A useful test is to write down what a user would see in the worst case, for example "the cart badge says 2 when it should say 3 for a second", and ask whether anyone would file a ticket or lose money over it.

sections.heading: What Stronger Consistency Costs
sections.body:
Each step toward stronger consistency generally costs latency (more round trips, waiting for quorum or synchronous confirmation), availability (per CAP, refusing requests during a partition), or both. This holds for every system, because "everyone sees the same, latest value" requires coordination between copies before you can answer, and coordination takes time and fails when nodes can't reach each other. Distance sets the floor: a round trip inside one region is around a millisecond, and one between the US East Coast and Europe is roughly 70 to 90 ms, so a synchronous cross-Atlantic write can't be faster than that however good the database is.

Eventual consistency is fast and resilient because it skips that coordination and accepts temporary disagreement. Better engineering can shrink the coordination cost, for example by placing replicas close together or keeping each customer's leader in their own region, but it can't remove it.

sections.heading: Reasoning About It as an Engineer (and in an Interview)
sections.body:
A practical checklist for "what consistency model should this feature use" questions: first, what does stale data cost the business? "Customer sees an old price for 2 seconds" is very different from "customer is double-charged." Second, what do latency or unavailability cost if you demand strong consistency? A checkout button that hangs at peak can be worse than brief staleness. Third, is there a cheaper middle ground: read-your-own-writes, bounded staleness, or strong consistency applied narrowly to just the critical path (the final balance check right before committing a transaction) while everything else about the same page is eventually consistent?

Products mix consistency levels per operation all the time. In an interview, name the operation before the level: "the stock check at checkout is strongly consistent, the badge on the listing page can be 30 seconds old" says far more than "we'll use a CP database."

examples.title: Quorum Reads and Writes
examples.code:
Cluster: N = 5 replicas total
Write: must be acknowledged by W = 3 replicas before returning success to the client
Read:  must be queried on R = 3 replicas, client takes the most recent value seen

Why W + R > N (3 + 3 = 6 > 5) guarantees the read sees the latest write:
  The write touched SOME set of 3 replicas out of 5.
  The read queries SOME set of 3 replicas out of 5, perhaps a different one.
  Two sets of size 3, drawn from a pool of 5, MUST overlap by at least 1
  (3 + 3 = 6, which is more than the 5 available slots -- by the pigeonhole
   principle, they can't be fully disjoint).
  At least 1 replica both recorded the write and answers the read, so the
  read sees that write (or something more recent).
examples.explanation: If W and R together exceed N, the set that acknowledged the write and the set that answers the read can't be disjoint, so at least one replica is in both, and the read picks its value because it is the most recent. You can shift the cost between the two sides: W=5, R=1 makes reads cheap but any single dead replica blocks writes, while W=3, R=3 tolerates two dead replicas for both. Cassandra exposes this per query (`QUORUM`, `ONE`, `ALL`), so one table can use quorums and another `ONE` for lower latency. DynamoDB descends from Amazon's Dynamo paper but doesn't expose W and R; it gives you a strongly consistent read flag. The overlap also assumes strict quorums: with "sloppy" quorums, where substitute nodes accept writes while the usual ones are down, the sets may not overlap.

examples.title: Sync vs. Async Replication: the Latency/Consistency Tradeoff
examples.code:
SYNCHRONOUS replication (leader waits for follower ack before confirming to client):
  Client write -> Leader -> [wait for Follower ack] -> Leader confirms to client
  Write latency: leader's write time + full round trip to follower + follower's write time
  Consistency: strong for that follower, IF it applies the write before acking -- then a
               read reaching it right after is current
  Cost: if the follower is slow, down, or unreachable (partition), the write STALLS or fails
        -> this is the CAP tradeoff: consistency purchased with availability

ASYNCHRONOUS replication (leader confirms immediately, replicates in background):
  Client write -> Leader -> Leader confirms to client immediately
                          -> (separately, in the background) Leader -> Follower
  Write latency: just the leader's own write time -- fast, unaffected by follower health
  Consistency: eventual -- follower catches up "soon," but a read hitting it right after
               the leader's confirmation can see the OLD value (replication lag)
  Cost: staleness window on followers; if leader fails before replicating, a write
        acknowledged to the client can be LOST if a follower is promoted without it
examples.explanation: With synchronous replication the client waits for two nodes to agree before hearing "done", so it pays in latency on every write and in availability when the follower is unreachable. Asynchronous replication skips the wait, and eventual consistency on the followers follows from that. The last line of the async block is the one teams forget: an acknowledged write can be lost on failover if the promoted follower hadn't received it. A common compromise is semi-synchronous: one of several followers must confirm (in Postgres, `synchronous_standby_names = 'ANY 1 (a, b)'`), so one slow follower doesn't stall writes, and losing the leader doesn't lose acknowledged data as long as you promote a follower that confirmed.

examples.title: Choosing Consistency Levels Across One Product
examples.code:
Feature                        Consistency level needed   Why
Bank account balance/transfer   Strong (linearizable or    A stale balance could approve a
                                 serialized transactions)   withdrawal that overdraws the account
User's own posted comment       Read-your-own-writes        Not seeing your own comment appear
  appearing on their own screen                              immediately feels broken, even if
                                                              other users seeing it a few seconds
                                                              later is completely fine
"Like" / view counter           Eventual                    Being off by a handful for a few
                                                              seconds is unnoticeable; volume is too
                                                              high to justify coordination cost
Product page price shown to a   Bounded staleness (short    A brief staleness window is a small,
  browsing customer              TTL cache, tens of secs)   bounded risk; strong consistency on every
                                                              page view adds latency to huge low-risk
                                                              read volume
examples.explanation: Each row is a cost-benefit calculation. The balance case picks strong consistency because the cost of being wrong (approving a bad transaction) vastly exceeds the cost of a slower write. The counter case picks eventual consistency because the cost of being wrong (a slightly off number) is trivially low and the volume/latency savings are large. The comment case picks read-your-own-writes because users notice when their own action doesn't show up, and nobody else is waiting for it. The price row works only because checkout reads the authoritative price again before charging; if the displayed price were the charged price, it would move to the top row.

misconceptions.description: Eventual consistency means the data is basically wrong or unreliable until it 'catches up' at some vague point.
misconceptions.clarification: Eventual consistency has a defined guarantee (given no new writes, all replicas converge) and buys lower write latency and continued availability when some nodes are slow, down, or partitioned. For features where brief staleness doesn't matter (counters, feeds, non-critical caches), it's often the better engineering choice, not a compromise and not consistency nobody got around to implementing. What it doesn't give you is a bound on how long convergence takes, so measure replication lag and alert on it.

misconceptions.description: Strong consistency is strictly better, so a well-engineered system should use it everywhere it can afford to.
misconceptions.clarification: Even when a system "can afford" the performance cost, strong consistency reduces availability under partition (per CAP) and adds coordination latency to every operation using it, including the many where nobody would have noticed staleness. Applied uniformly, you pay that on every read of a "like" counter and every view of a rarely changing product description, for a guarantee those operations never needed. Decide per operation.

exercises.prompt: A key-value store has N=5 replicas. It's configured with W=1 (a write only needs to be acknowledged by 1 replica) and R=1 (a read only needs to query 1 replica). A client writes value 'X=new', which is acknowledged after reaching only replica 3. Immediately after, a different client reads X, and the read happens to query replica 1. Predict what the read returns, and explain whether this configuration guarantees the read-after-write scenario works.
exercises.code:
N = 5 replicas: [replica1, replica2, replica3, replica4, replica5]
W = 1, R = 1  (W + R = 2, which is NOT greater than N = 5)

Write "X=new" -> acknowledged by replica3 only (W=1 satisfied)
Read X -> queries replica1 only (R=1 satisfied)
hints: Check the W + R > N condition from the quorum example -- does it hold here? What does that tell you about whether overlap between the write's replica and the read's replica is GUARANTEED?
With W=1, only ONE specific replica (replica3) actually has the new value immediately -- have the other 4 replicas necessarily received it yet?
The read queried replica1, not replica3. Is there any guarantee connecting those two specific replicas in this configuration?
exercises.expectedAnswer: The read very likely returns the OLD value of X. Only replica3 had to acknowledge the write (W=1); the other 4 replicas, including replica1, receive it asynchronously, so there is no guarantee replica1 has it yet. Since W + R = 1 + 1 = 2, which is NOT greater than N = 5, nothing forces the write set and the read set to overlap, and here they didn't: {replica3} and {replica1}.
exercises.solutionExplanation: With W=1 and R=1, the system is configured for minimum latency and maximum availability, and gives up any guarantee linking a given read to a given write. The overlap argument needs W + R > N; 2 is far short of 5, so a write can land on replica3 while a read is served by replica1, which may receive that write milliseconds or minutes later. In a Dynamo-style store the write is usually sent to all 5 replicas at once and W only says how many to wait for, so the read often does see the new value, which hides the problem in testing. The configuration is valid for data that tolerates it, such as a metrics buffer or a cache. If this read must see that write, raise W and R until W + R > N (3 and 3, for example), accepting that each operation now waits for three replicas. W=1 also has a durability cost: if replica3 dies before passing the write on, it is gone.

exercises.prompt: A team builds a flash-sale feature: 10,000 users can attempt to buy 1 of 50 remaining units of a product at the same instant. They use an eventually-consistent, leaderless data store with W=1, R=1 for the 'units remaining' counter, reasoning 'we used the same fast setup as our other counters, like counts.' Some customers are charged for units that don't exist (the store oversold to 340 orders against 50 units). Diagnose the mistake in reasoning, and describe the fix.
exercises.code:
# Fragment: inventory_store is a hypothetical leaderless client
inventory_store.configure(N=5, W=1, R=1)   # same config used for "like" counters elsewhere

def attempt_purchase(product_id):
    remaining = inventory_store.read(f"inventory:{product_id}")   # R=1, possibly stale
    if remaining > 0:
        inventory_store.decrement(f"inventory:{product_id}")      # W=1, not globally coordinated
        return "purchase confirmed"
    return "sold out"
hints: 'Like' counts and 'units remaining before overselling' look similar (both are numbers going up/down under concurrent writes) -- but is the COST of being wrong the same for both?

With W=1, R=1 and thousands of concurrent decrement attempts, is there anything stopping two different requests from both reading 'remaining=1' from two different replicas and both proceeding to purchase?
This needs the read-check-decrement sequence to be safe against concurrent execution -- what kind of consistency/coordination mechanism guarantees that, that W=1/R=1 does not provide?
exercises.solutionCode:
# Fragment: hypothetical API
# FIX: use a strongly consistent, coordinated decrement -- e.g. a conditional
# atomic operation backed by quorum or a single authoritative node for this key,
# not independent read-then-write against arbitrary replicas.

def attempt_purchase(product_id):
    # atomic conditional decrement: succeeds ONLY if remaining > 0,
    # evaluated and applied as one indivisible, strongly-consistent operation
    # (e.g. a quorum-backed compare-and-swap, or routed through a single
    # authoritative leader for this specific key)
    success = inventory_store.atomic_decrement_if_positive(
        f"inventory:{product_id}", consistency="strong"
    )
    return "purchase confirmed" if success else "sold out"
exercises.solutionExplanation: The mistake is treating "a number that changes under concurrent access" as one category, when what decides is the cost of being wrong. Nobody notices a "like" count that is briefly off; overselling means 290 customers (340 - 50) charged for units that don't exist. With W=1, R=1, concurrent runs of attempt_purchase are not coordinated: thousands of requests can each read a 'remaining' value from whichever replica they reach, see 'remaining > 0', and all proceed to decrement before any of the decrements is visible. Raising W and R to quorums would not be enough, because two requests can still both read 1, both pass the check, and both decrement; the check and the decrement have to be one step. So the fix is an atomic, strongly consistent conditional decrement: a compare-and-swap run through consensus (Cassandra's lightweight transactions), a DynamoDB conditional update, or one authoritative node such as `UPDATE inventory SET remaining = remaining - 1 WHERE product_id = ? AND remaining > 0` in a relational database, checking that one row was affected. After 50 successes, the 51st attempt sees the depleted count and returns 'sold out'.

assessments.prompt: A team is deciding on a consistency model for a 'number of views' counter shown on video pages, which is read/written extremely frequently and where being off by a small amount for a few seconds is completely unnoticeable to users. Which choice best matches the requirement?
options: Strong consistency (linearizable reads/writes), because correctness should always be maximized regardless of the feature.
There is no valid consistency choice for a value that changes this frequently -- it must be recalculated from scratch on every page load.

Eventual consistency, because the cost of brief, small staleness is negligible for this feature, and the high read/write volume makes the latency and coordination cost of strong consistency expensive for no real benefit.
Sharding the counter across multiple databases, since that is the standard fix for any consistency problem.
assessments.explanation: Very high read/write volume and a negligible cost of brief staleness suit eventual consistency. Strong consistency would add latency to every view and reduce availability under partition for a guarantee this feature doesn't need. The “Strong consistency (linearizable reads/writes), because correctness should…” option ignores what strong consistency costs; here it trades performance for something no viewer would notice. The “Sharding the counter across multiple databases, since…” option confuses sharding (a tool for write/data-size scaling) with a consistency-model decision. The “There is no valid consistency choice…” option is false: eventually consistent counters are a standard pattern and don't require recomputation from scratch.

assessments.prompt: Explain why 'is this system consistent?' is not really a well-formed question, and what a more useful question looks like, using at least two concrete features as examples.
assessments.modelAnswer: 'Is this system consistent?' treats consistency as one yes-or-no property of an entire system, but systems with replication and sharding almost always give different guarantees to different operations. A single product might use strong consistency for a payment or balance update, because a stale read there could approve a transaction against money that isn't there, which is worth extra write latency and reduced availability under partition. The same product might use eventual consistency for a 'like' counter, because being off by a handful for a few seconds is invisible to users, while the read/write volume is enormous and coordinating every increment would be expensive. And it might use an in-between guarantee, read-your-own-writes, for a user's newly posted comment, because users notice if their own action doesn't show up, though they'd never notice if a different user's view of that comment lagged by a second or two. A more useful question, asked per operation, is: 'what guarantee does this read or write need, given the cost of it being wrong, and what am I willing to pay in latency or availability to get it?' Answering it takes knowledge of the mechanisms (quorum configuration, synchronous vs. asynchronous replication) and of what staleness costs the business for that feature. Stronger is not always better, and weaker is not always an acceptable shortcut.

assessments.prompt: A cluster has N=5 replicas, configured with W=3 and R=3. Why does this configuration guarantee a read will see the most recent write?
options: Because with W=3 and R=3, all 5 replicas are updated synchronously before the write is acknowledged.

Because W + R (3 + 3 = 6) exceeds N (5), so the set of replicas acknowledging the write and the set of replicas queried by the read cannot be fully disjoint -- at least one replica must belong to both sets and will have recorded the write.
Because the write is always sent to the same 3 replicas that the read later queries, by convention.
Because 3 out of 5 replicas is a majority, and majorities are defined to always be up to date.
assessments.explanation: By the pigeonhole principle, two sets of size 3 drawn from a pool of 5 cannot be fully disjoint, since 3+3=6 exceeds 5, so at least one replica must be common to both the write's acknowledging set and the read's querying set. The “Because 3 out of 5 replicas…” option invents a property of majorities; a majority can be stale unless it overlaps the write set. The “Because the write is always sent…” option is false: the replicas can differ each time, and the overlap holds whichever ones are chosen. The “Because with W=3 and R=3, all 5…” option is wrong: with W=3, only 3 of the 5 replicas need to acknowledge the write.

assessments.prompt: What is the risk of asynchronous replication that is easy to forget when only thinking about read staleness?
options: If the leader fails before a write has replicated to a follower, and that follower is then promoted to leader, an already-acknowledged write can be lost entirely, rather than only delayed.
Asynchronous replication requires twice the network bandwidth of synchronous replication under all conditions, so a leader under heavy load will eventually fall behind on every request it receives.
Asynchronous replication makes every write permanently unrecoverable, even before any failure occurs.
Asynchronous replication prevents the system from ever using quorum reads or writes.
assessments.explanation: If the leader fails before replicating and a follower without the write is promoted, the write is gone even though the client was told it succeeded. That is data loss, a different problem from the better-known replication lag. The “Asynchronous replication makes every write permanently unrecoverable…” option overstates it: most writes do replicate, and the risk is limited to the window before they do. The “Asynchronous replication requires twice the network bandwidth…” option is fabricated: both modes ship the same data. The “Asynchronous replication prevents the system from ever…” option is false: a store can replicate in the background and still let a read or write wait for a quorum.

assessments.prompt: Why is applying strong consistency to every operation in a system, including a rarely-changing product description page, considered a mistake even if the system "can afford" the performance cost?
options: Because strong consistency can only be applied to numeric fields, not text content like product descriptions.
Because strong consistency is technically impossible to implement for read-only pages.
Because product description pages are always sharded, and sharded data cannot use strong consistency.
Because it pays coordination latency and reduced availability under partition on every operation.
assessments.explanation: Strong consistency reduces availability under partition and adds coordination latency to every operation that uses it. A product description that changes twice a year gains nothing visible in return, so the cost is paid on every view for a guarantee nobody needed. The “Because strong consistency is technically impossible…” option is false: it can be implemented for read-only pages; the objection is that it isn't worth the cost. The “Because strong consistency can only be applied…” and “Because product description pages are always sharded…” options are fabricated: consistency doesn't depend on field type, and sharded stores can offer strong consistency per key or across shards.
